div.head: Ine 19
div.ab: Cyninges geneat, gif his wer bið CXX scll', he mot swerigan for LX hida, gif he bið huslgenga.
LXIII. Cyninges geneat, gif his wer bið twelfhund scill., he mot swerian for syxtig hida, gif he bið huslgengea.

Regis geneat (id est uillanus [colonus fiscalinus]) si wera eius sit twelfhund scill. (id est duodecies C sol.), potest iurare pro LX hidis (id est pro sex hominibus), si sit hulsgenga (id est duodecimhindus uel husbonda).
{LXIII} Cyninges geneat, gif his wer bið twelfhund sciƚƚ, he mot swerian for syxtig hida, gif he bið huslgenga.
A member of the king’s household, if his wer is 1,200 shillings, may swear [an oath in the value of] sixty hides, if he is a communicant.
A member of the king's household if his wergeld is 1200 shillings, shall be allowed to swear for 60 hides, if he is a communicant.
A king’s geneat, if his wergild is 1200 shillings, may, if he is a communicant, swear for 60 hides.
Ein Königs-Gefolgsmann, wenn sein Wergeld 1200 Schill. beträgt, der darf schwören für 60 Hiden, vorausgesetzt, er sei Abendmahlsgänger.
A king’s retainer, if his wergeld amounts to 1200 shillings, may swear for 60 hides, provided he is a communicant.

note.label: contrast
note.quote: But see §21 for evidence that the term can also apply to those of lower rank.

div.note: This word denotes originally “a member of a household” and may in these early laws be being used quite generally. By the eleventh century it is used of men who hold land from a lord and pay rent and certain honourable services (especially riding duties), and who seem to correspond to a class called “radcnihts” in Domesday Book. In its technical sense a geneat differs from a gesith in not normally being of the noble class. On gesith, see p. 396, n. 4. 1
